title: Quadragesimo Anno (1931)
hook: Moses is judging every case alone until his father-in-law steps in, and a pope later gives the advice a name

segments.voice: Yesterday, Leo's letter again, and a worker worthy of his hire. Your line was a just wage. Did you find the number, and hold it next to someone's pay? Day one thousand three hundred one.

From morning until night, the people stand around Moses, waiting for him to settle their disputes. Every case, large or small, comes to one man. His father-in-law Jethro watches a day of it and tells him plainly, in Exodus, that this isn't good: he'll wear himself out, and the people with him. Choose capable, honest people, Jethro says. Set them over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens. Let them judge the small matters, and bring the hard ones to you. Moses listens. Much later, a pope wrote a letter that gave Jethro's kind of advice a name. Today, Quadragesimo Anno.
screen: `ONE MAN, EVERY CASE.` → `JETHRO: THIS ISN'T GOOD.` → `SHARE THE LOAD.`

segments.voice: First, the letter. Quadragesimo anno is Latin for in the fortieth year. Pius the Eleventh opens his letter by marking forty years since Leo's Rerum Novarum, looks back at what that letter set moving, and takes up questions it left open. Second, the principle he states, which the Church now calls subsidiarity. Pius writes that it's an injustice, and a disturbance of right order, for a larger and higher body to take over what a smaller one can do for itself. What a family can decide, the city shouldn't decide for it. What a town can handle, a national government shouldn't swallow. Third, it cuts both ways. Subsidiarity isn't simply small is good. Pius also says that every social body exists to help its members, and never to destroy or absorb them. So when the smaller group can't manage, when a family can't build a hospital or a village can't fight a flood alone, the larger body has a duty to step in and help. The Catechism puts it as support and coordination for the sake of the common good. Help from above that strengthens the hands below, rather than replacing them. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary Tuesday. Subsidiarity is a form of respect. It trusts the people closest to a problem to know something about it. The manager who lets the team decide how to reach the goal. The parent who lets a teenager plan the trip. The parish that asks the volunteers who run the food pantry before rewriting its rules. Moses wasn't weaker for sharing the load. Jethro's promise, in Exodus, was that the people would go home in peace.
screen: `IN THE FORTIETH YEAR.` · `DON'T TAKE WHAT THE SMALLER CAN DO.` · `THE LARGER EXISTS TO HELP.` · then, large: `TRUST THE PEOPLE CLOSEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let a group decide. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a group where you usually make the call. A team at work. Your household. A committee, a class, a group chat planning a weekend. Find one decision there that the people closest to it could make without you. Picture handing it over, cleanly, and offering help only if they ask. If there's an urge to take it back, notice it, and let it pass. If you pray, you can ask God for that kind of trust. The bell holds the time.
Quadragesimo Anno. In the fortieth year: Pius the Eleventh's letter after Rerum Novarum, which states the principle of subsidiarity. Today's word.
Your line: from the ground up. Today, let one decision be made by the people closest to it, and help only if they ask. Day one thousand three hundred one.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching applies subsidiarity to families, parishes, schools and governments, and Catholics cite it in debates over which level of society should take on a task.

fork.setup: you're Moses, settling the people's disputes from morning until night. your father-in-law says you'll wear yourself out. what do you do?
options: keep going: only you can judge rightly.
appoint capable people over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens.
stop judging and let the people sort it out alone.
fork.reveal: Moses takes Jethro's advice: small matters are judged close to home, and the hard ones come to him. sharing the load, not dropping it.

original.note: Latin: in the fortieth year. the opening words of Pius XI's letter, and so its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a Latin title nobody remembers.
what it means: in the fortieth year: Pius XI's letter after Rerum Novarum, which states the principle of decisions made from the ground up.
what a scholar hears: the principle of subsidiary function: larger bodies exist to help smaller ones, and must never destroy or absorb them.

notes: 'Forty years since Rerum Novarum' rests on Quadragesimo Anno 1, which opens by marking forty years; the year 1931 is kept in the title only and not stated in the voice.

Quadragesimo Anno 79–80 paraphrased (it is an injustice and a disturbance of right order to assign to a greater and higher association what lesser bodies can do; social activity should help members, never destroy or absorb them). Pius calls it the principle of 'subsidiary function'; the lesson says the Church 'now calls' it subsidiarity. Confirm.
Exodus 18 paraphrased; the numbers (thousands, hundreds, fifties, tens) are from 18:21. 'The people went home in peace' paraphrases 18:23; confirm against the Douay-Rheims wording.
'Pius looks back ... and takes up questions it left open' is a general description of the letter; confirm.
Editor: Exodus 18:23 is Jethro's promise that the people will go home in peace, not a narrated outcome; fixed. 'Morning until evening' now 'morning until night' to match Exodus 18:13.
